title: EmoTrace-Bench: Diagnosing Emotional Expression in Text-to-Video Generation through Controlled Cues and Intensity

paper.title: EmoTrace-Bench: Diagnosing Emotional Expression in Text-to-Video Generation through Controlled Cues and Intensity
paper.abstract: Abstract Text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly used to generate videos with targeted emotional expressions, yet existing evaluation methods mainly rely on holistic video–text alignment and provide limited insight into whether failures arise from target-emotion expression, intensity control, or specific affective cues. We introduce EmoTrace-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark that controls emotion intensity and selected affective cues in prompts and evaluates generated videos at multiple levels. EmoTrace-Bench contains 448 controlled prompts covering eight emotions, two intensity levels, and diverse cue conditions. Using 12 T2V models, we generate 5,376 videos and evaluate target-emotion presence, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual dimensions of emotional expression with an automated evaluator calibrated and validated against human annotations on a subset of the data. Results reveal substantial differences across models and prompt designs. Prompts that explicitly describe a character’s emotional reaction are followed more reliably than prompts that describe only events or scenes, whereas adding more affective cues or using more explicit cinematic audiovisual language does not consistently improve emotional generation. These results illustrate how aggregate alignment scores may overlook localized differences in target-emotion expression, intensity control, and cue realization. EmoTrace-Bench provides a traceable and interpretable framework for diagnosing emotional video generation without modifying existing generation pipelines, and we release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: EmoTrace-Bench at a glance. Left: the three-level evaluation taxonomy—whether the target emotion is expressed, whether its perceived intensity is weak or strong, and which of ten expression channels (character, visual form, audio, context, temporal) provide the evidence. Top right: correct content does not guarantee emotional expression; a model must infer the emotion from context and reaction and realize the requested intensity, and existing benchmarks do not diagnose where this fails. Bottom right: the four capability facets examined in Section 4—breadth across emotions and prompt conditions, depth of intensity control and cue support, and explicit versus implicit cue expression. Generating videos with explicit emotional expression is an important capability for controllable content generation in text-to-video (T2V) models. For controllable emotion generation, the key question is not only whether a video presents the target emotion, but also whether it follows the prompt’s requirements regarding the emotion category, emotion intensity, and specific expressive cues. Emotion generation in T2V is therefore not a single-dimensional problem; rather, it simultaneously involves multiple interrelated yet distinguishable capabilities, including emotion category, emotion intensity, and specific emotional cues. However, existing T2V evaluations have difficulty effectively distinguishing these capabilities. Existing multidimensional video generation benchmarks mainly focus on semantic consistency, visual quality, motion performance, and compositional relationships, and they generally lack explicit modeling of emotional expression ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ) . The few works oriented toward emotion generation also mostly use aggregate scores to measure the overall match between generated videos and emotion prompts ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) . Although these metrics can indicate whether a video aligns with its prompt overall, they provide limited insight into the specific causes of mismatches and may collapse qualitatively different generation errors into similar aggregate scores, thereby obscuring meaningful differences in models’ ability to follow fine-grained emotional instructions. As a result, such evaluations cannot fully characterize a model’s controllability over emotion category, intensity, and mode of expression in practical content creation. Adding more output-side metrics alone is insufficient, because confounds often arise during prompt construction. Emotional prompts typically combine multiple cues, making it difficult to attribute output changes to specific factors. Differences across emotion categories can further confound intensity comparisons. Reliable diagnosis therefore requires controlled inputs as well as fine-grained outputs. We propose EmoTrace-Bench (Figure 1 ), which treats prompts as controlled experimental variables. It varies two main factors: affective cues and emotion intensity. Cue-controlled prompts change only one cue phrase while keeping the rest fixed, with additional paraphrased variants to test sensitivity to wording. Intensity-controlled prompt pairs differ only in intensity-related terms while preserving the emotion category, scene, and other content. This design enables separate analysis of emotion category, intensity, and specific cues. Figure 2 summarizes the overall pipeline. At the output, we annotate target-emotion success, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual cue dimensions. Using 448 controlled prompts, we generate 5,376 videos from 12 T2V models and collect human annotations for 1,120 videos from three of them to validate the automated evaluation. The analysis reveals that emotion-category generation and intensity control are distinct capabilities, model performance can be sensitive to cue wording, and automated evaluation agrees broadly with human judgments while small systematic differences remain on some fine-grained dimensions. By controlling variables at the input and conducting fine-grained diagnosis at the output, EmoTrace-Bench decomposes emotion-generation performance that was previously mixed together in overall scores into more specific dimensions and prompt factors. At the same time, through per-video, per-attribute comparisons between human and automated evaluation, it further reveals the scope of applicability and limitations of automated evaluation across different emotional dimensions. The main contributions of this paper are threefold: (i) We introduce EmoTrace-Bench , a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark for emotion generation in text-to-video models. It decomposes emotion generation into three complementary levels: emotion category, emotion intensity, and ten affective cue channels, enabling localized diagnosis of generation failures. (ii) We develop a controlled prompt-construction framework that independently varies emotion intensity and affective cues under a minimal-difference design. It also includes semantically matched cue variants with different linguistic realizations, allowing us to study prompt sensitivity while reducing confounding across input factors. (iii) We benchmark 12 text-to-video models on 448 controlled prompts, yielding 5,376 generated videos, and collect human annotations for 1,120 videos to validate the automated evaluation protocol. Our analysis reveals substantial differences across models in emotion-category generation, intensity control, and prompt sensitivity, while showing that aggregate automated judgments are broadly aligned with human annotations. We release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules.

sections.heading: 2.1 Text-to-Video Generation Evaluation
sections.text: T2V evaluation has evolved from overall quality assessment toward multidimensional diagnosis. VBench, VBench++, VBench-2.0, EvalCrafter, and Video-Bench evaluate visual quality, motion, temporal consistency, subject consistency, spatial relations, text alignment, and higher-level generation fidelity ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ) . VABench and T2AV-Compass further consider audio quality and audiovisual consistency ( Hua et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) , while T2V-CompBench uses controlled prompts to evaluate compositional generation ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Despite this progress, these benchmarks mainly target general generation quality, semantic adherence, and compositionality. Emotional expression is rarely modeled as a structured capability with separable dimensions. Existing evaluations therefore provide limited diagnosis of whether errors arise from emotion category, intensity, or specific character, scene, and audiovisual cues.

sections.heading: 2.2 Emotional Video Generation and Controllable Expression
sections.text: Recent work has begun to study emotion-aware video generation. EmoVid provides a multimodal dataset for emotion-centric video understanding and generation ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) ; FG-ECVG explores fine-grained controllable emotional video generation ( Wei et al., 2025 ) ; and EmoTalker studies editable emotional expression in talking-face generation ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . EmoWorld further disentangles atmosphere, affective semantic cues, and temporal progression, showing that video emotion contains multiple controllable components ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . These works mainly focus on emotional data, generation, or model-side control. Their evaluations still commonly rely on emotion-recognition accuracy, condition matching, or aggregate scores. Such metrics may assign similar scores to different failures, such as generating the correct emotion at the wrong intensity or creating an appropriate atmosphere without the requested facial or bodily expression. Thus, an overall emotion score is insufficient for diagnosing fine-grained emotional controllability.

sections.heading: 2.3 Fine-Grained Emotional and Audiovisual Cues
sections.text: Emotion is conveyed through multiple channels. Psychological studies highlight the roles of facial expression, body posture, and movement ( Ekman & Friesen, 1978 ; Cohn et al., 2007 ; Coulson, 2004 ; Dael et al., 2012a ; Dael et al., 2012b ; Aviezer et al., 2012 ) , while film studies show that shot scale, motion, lighting, color, sound, and music also shape emotional perception ( Bálint et al., 2018 ; Detenber et al., 1998 ; Chion, 1994 ; Cohen, 2010 ; Bordwell et al., 2020 ) . Recent benchmarks such as Stable Cinemetrics and FilmBench evaluate structured cinematic attributes ( Chatterjee et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , while HVEval and HUG-VIS examine human-centered appearance, action, and emotion ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Building on these directions, EmoTrace-Bench decomposes emotion generation into emotion category, emotion intensity, and specific affective cues. It combines controlled prompts with fine-grained output evaluation to diagnose whether the target emotion is generated, whether its intensity follows the prompt, and through which character, scene, and audiovisual cues it is expressed. This moves emotion-generation evaluation from holistic matching toward traceable fine-grained diagnosis. sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of the EmoTrace-Bench pipeline. Prompts from the controlled suite (top) are sent unchanged to every model; the middle row shows matched weak/strong generations for one fear prompt pair across models. All videos are scored by a single automated evaluator that is frozen after calibration against human labels (left) and applied through the two-stage affective evaluation (bottom).

sections.heading: 3.1 Evaluation Target Design
sections.text: EmoTrace-Bench evaluates emotional video generation at three levels: target emotion, perceived intensity, and affective cues. We first define the target emotion set and then specify the audiovisual dimensions used for fine-grained diagnosis. Selection of Eight Emotions. EmoTrace-Bench includes eight emotions: amusement, excitement, awe, contentment, anger, fear, disgust, and sadness. The selection follows the discrete emotion set established by Mikels et al. using the International Affective Picture System (IAPS) ( Mikels et al., 2005 ) . It contains four positive and four negative emotions spanning different typical arousal levels ( Russell, 1980 ) . Three-Level Evaluation. For each generated video, the first level determines whether the target emotion is expressed. The second evaluates perceived emotion intensity as strong or weak when the target emotion is present, and as “not matched” otherwise. The third identifies which audiovisual cue dimensions support the target emotion. These levels capture whether the intended emotion is expressed, how strongly it is expressed, and through which cues. Multidimensional Affective Cues. Emotional expression in video can arise from character behavior, environmental context, and audiovisual form. Drawing on theories of emotional expression, film form, and an external inventory of affective cues ( Smith, 2003 ) , we define ten dimensions: facial expression, bodily behavior, lighting, color, composition, visual dynamics, temporal organization, sound, scene, and event. We retain cues that can be directly observed and judged relatively independently in short videos, while excluding factors that require long-form narrative, dialogue semantics, or broader temporal context. Operational definitions and channel-specific prerequisites are provided in Appendix C (Table C.1 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Controlled Prompt Set
sections.text: EmoTrace-Bench uses controlled prompts to vary emotion intensity, affective cues, and prompt formulation while minimizing unrelated changes across conditions. Scale and Structure. Each prompt is represented as P ⁡ ( e , s , i , t ) = B ⁡ ( e , s ) + I ⁡ ( e , i ) + ∑ d ∈ ℳ t C d , t ​ ( e , s ) , P(e,s,i,t)=B(e,s)+I(e,i)+\sum_{d\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}C_{d,t}(e,s), where e e is the target emotion, s s the scene, i i the intensity level, and t t the prompt template. B ⁡ ( e , s ) B(e,s) is the shared base description, I ⁡ ( e , i ) I(e,i) specifies emotion intensity, and C d , t ​ ( e , s ) C_{d,t}(e,s) denotes the realization of affective cue d d under template t t . The template determines which cue segments are included through ℳ t \mathcal{M}_{t} and, for selected conditions, how the same affective content is linguistically expressed. The benchmark crosses 8 emotions, 2 intensity levels with 2 samples each, and 14 prompt templates, yielding 448 prompts. The templates include emotion-only prompts, individual facial, bodily, scene, and event cues, combinations of character and environmental cues, alternative linguistic realizations, facial changes, empty scenes, and prompts containing all explicitly writable cues. Eight of the ten evaluation dimensions—facial expression, bodily behavior, lighting, color, composition, visual dynamics, scene, and event—can be explicitly specified in prompts. Temporal organization and sound are evaluated only in the generated video. Each prompt records whether a cue dimension is explicitly specified or left unspecified but observable, allowing explicit instruction following to be distinguished from cues that emerge without being requested. Representative prompt conditions are shown in Figure B.1 in Appendix B . Alternative Linguistic Realizations. To examine sensitivity to prompt formulation, we construct controlled prompt pairs that express similar affective content using different linguistic realizations. These pairs preserve the target emotion, scene, and intended affective content while changing how that content is described. They therefore allow us to test whether semantically similar instructions lead to different generation outcomes. Prompt Control and Validation. We apply three constraints to reduce unintended variation. First, strong–weak pairs share the same emotion, scene, base description, and template and differ only in preregistered intensity expressions; all 224 / 224 224/224 pairs pass character-level structural verification. Second, cue segments are reused across templates whenever possible. Of 384 reused segments, 372 are identical and 12 differ only in pronoun disambiguation; all 384 match after normalization. Third, controlled template pairs vary only the preregistered prompt factor, and all 448 prompts have unique SHA-256 hashes. These checks (Table B.4 ) establish structural consistency for controlled comparisons.

sections.heading: 3.3 Automated Evaluation and Human Annotation Protocol
sections.text: Automated evaluation and human annotation follow the same three-level decision structure and information boundaries. Shared Evaluation Protocol. Both evaluators first determine whether the target emotion is present. If present, perceived intensity is labeled as strong or weak; otherwise it is labeled “not matched.” Each of the ten affective cue dimensions is then judged independently as present or absent in support of the target emotion. Emotion and intensity are judged directly and are not inferred from cue labels. Both evaluators see only the generated video, including its native audio, and the name and definition of the target emotion. They do not have access to the generation prompt or other metadata. The target emotion is provided because the task evaluates whether a specified emotion is expressed. The target intensity is hidden to reduce label-following bias. Automated Evaluation. All 5,376 videos are evaluated once using Gemini 3.1 Pro with temperature 0 under a frozen two-stage protocol: the first stage judges target emotion and perceived intensity, and the second stage judges the ten cue channels (Appendix C ). Videos are sampled at 8 fps. Auxiliary programs provide measurement summaries for visual dynamics and sound using cross-frame motion and audio features, respectively. The resulting single-run outputs are used for all 12-model benchmark results. To assess evaluator stability, we conduct two additional evaluation runs on the 896-video development set. Development-set validity results are reported as the mean over the three runs (Appendix D ). Wan-2.2, HunyuanVideo-1.5, Kandinsky-5.0-T2V-Pro, and LongCat-Video-13.6B do not provide usable native audio, so the sound dimension and Full 10D aggregate are not reported for these models. Human Reference and Consensus. The human reference contains a development set for protocol calibration and a held-out test set for cross-generator validation. All first-pass annotations are collected without access to automated evaluation outputs. The development set contains 896 videos from two generation models. Two senior annotators independently label all videos. Their matching labels form the first-pass consensus, while disagreements are resolved by the majority of available labels from five additional trained annotators (Appendix D ). The test set contains 224 videos from a third generation model and was not used in protocol development. Two trained annotators provide full first-pass annotations and form the initial consensus. After the automated evaluator is frozen, senior annotators conduct a second review of both sets (Appendix D ). Reviewers see only the video and decision rules, without access to the generation prompt, model identity, target intensity, or automated outputs. Reviewed labels form the reviewed human reference, and fields without a reviewed label are excluded from analyses against it. Metric Computation. The joint emotion-and-intensity score is computed over all 448 videos per model. Visual 9D averages cue support over the nine non-audio channels and is available for all models; Full 10D adds the sound channel and is therefore reported only for audio-capable models (Appendix C ). Both are computed only for videos that successfully express the target emotion and should therefore be interpreted together with target-emotion accuracy. “Undecided” and “not applicable” labels are excluded from the corresponding denominators.

sections.heading: 4 Results and Analysis
sections.text: We analyze EmoTrace-Bench from three perspectives. First, we compare 12 T2V models in terms of target-emotion generation, intensity control, and cue realization. Second, we use controlled prompt pairs to examine the effects of cue specification, cue combination, and linguistic realization. Third, we assess the reliability of the automated evaluator through comparisons with human judgments and an alternative evaluator backbone.

sections.heading: 4.1 Emotion Generation and Intensity Control
sections.text: The 12 models exhibit distinct capability profiles. Target-emotion accuracy ranges from 49.3% to 87.0%, joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy from 29.9% to 55.1%, and conditional Visual 9D expression depth from 62.7% to 83.5%. Paired intensity-control success is substantially lower, ranging from 10.3% to 29.5%. Taken together, these results suggest that models are generally more successful at expressing the target emotion than at reliably controlling its perceived intensity. Figure 3 (a) summarizes the overall model results. Prompt-level paired bootstrap analysis of target-emotion accuracy (Appendix C ) yields six bootstrap-based groups of models for which no significant within-group differences are detected under the adopted procedure. Seedance-2.5 and Veo-3.1 form the highest-performing group. These differences are not an artifact of generation seed. Regenerating all 448 videos for Kling-3.0 under three generation seeds, with prompts and all other exposed settings fixed, moves target-emotion accuracy by 3.6 points (72.5–76.1%) and joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy by 3.8 points (45.5–49.3%), with no pairwise difference significant under exact McNemar tests (Appendix A.3 ). For this model and these three seed settings, the observed score ranges are approximately 7–11 times smaller than the corresponding cross-model spreads. Performance also varies across emotion categories (Figure 3 (b)). Contentment (85.9%) and amusement (85.3%) achieve the highest average target-emotion accuracy, whereas anger (52.2%) and fear (59.8%) are the lowest. Across the emotion categories included in our benchmark, the four positive emotions achieve 17.7 percentage points higher target-emotion accuracy on average than the four negative emotions, with the difference consistent in direction across all 12 models. Intensity control exhibits a different failure pattern. Across models, 17.9%–48.2% of strong–weak pairs receive the same perceived intensity, whereas reversals occur in at most 5.8% of pairs (Table E.3 , Appendix E ). Thus, when intensity control fails, it is much more often because strong and weak prompts produce the same perceived intensity. Figure 3: Emotion generation across 12 T2V models. (a) Overall performance: target-emotion accuracy (Emotion), joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy (Emotion + intensity; E+I in the text), Visual 9D and Full 10D cue support, and bootstrap group; models within a group are not ordered. (b) Target-emotion accuracy for each of the eight emotions. Scores are obtained from one blinded automated evaluation per video. Cue-level results reveal additional cross-model differences (Figure 4 , left; Table E.1 , Appendix E ). Visual dynamics shows the largest variation across models, followed by event/reaction, sound, and lighting, whereas temporal organization and facial expression vary less. Because human–automated agreement is only moderate for composition and scene/space (Appendix D ), we report these two channels descriptively without further cross-model interpretation. Overall, target-emotion generation, intensity control, and cue realization capture different aspects of model behavior. These results motivate reporting these dimensions separately rather than collapsing them into a single aggregate score.

sections.heading: 4.2 Effects of Controlled Prompt Design
sections.text: We next examine how model outputs change under controlled prompt variations. The analysis focuses on three factors: explicit cue specification, cue combination, and linguistic realization. Per-model results for all 14 templates are reported in Table E.4 (Appendix E ).

sections.heading: Explicit Cue Specification.
sections.text: Explicitly specifying character reactions produces the largest and most consistent gains. Adding a character reaction to a scene-only prompt improves joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy by 25–59 percentage points across models, with a mean gain of 45 points. Adding a reaction to an event prompt yields a 22–69 point gain, with a mean of 46 points. After Holm correction, these improvements are significant for 9/12 and 7/12 models, respectively. Current models therefore follow explicit facial and bodily reactions more reliably than they infer such reactions from scene or event context alone. For cues that are not explicitly specified, we still record whether they appear in the generated video. Figure 4 compares overall cue support with support under unspecified conditions. These results characterize cue co-occurrence only and do not support causal interpretation. Figure 4: Overall (left) and implicit (right) cue-expression profiles of 12 T2V models. Values are relative to the best model in each channel.

sections.heading: Cue Combination.
sections.text: The benefit of adding a cue depends on which cue is added, not on how many are present. Adding a facial expression to a body-only prompt raises joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy from 40% to 64% on average (+24 points; significant for 2/12 models), whereas adding bodily behavior to a facial-expression prompt adds only 7 points (57% to 64%; significant for no model). Descriptively, facial expression contributes more than bodily behavior in this contrast. Likewise, the template that combines all explicitly writable cues (ALL_DYNAMIC, 64%) performs no better than the face-and-body prompt and only 2 points above the emotion-label baseline (EMO, 62%; Table E.4 ).

sections.heading: Alternative Linguistic Realizations.
sections.text: Describing a scene by how it feels conveys emotion more effectively than specifying how it should be filmed. With a character present, experiential atmosphere descriptions reach 27% joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy on average, compared with 13% for matched cinematic instructions; 9/12 models favor the experiential form, 2/12 significantly after correction. In empty scenes the two formulations perform alike (38% vs. 37%). For short, single-scene prompts of this kind, experiential language elicited emotional expression more often in our data. All pre-specified contrasts use exact paired McNemar tests with model-wise Holm correction (Table B.3 ). Because each condition contains 32 videos (16 strong–weak pairs), we read these comparisons as diagnostic evidence of how models respond to specific prompt changes.

sections.heading: 4.3 Agreement Between Automated and Human Evaluation
sections.text: Because the preceding analyses rely on automated scores, we compare the automated evaluator with human judgments at both the annotation and model levels. The evaluation uses a development set of 896 videos and a test set of 224 videos from a third generation model, held out from protocol development.

sections.heading: Human Agreement.
sections.text: On the development set, pairwise human agreement is 85.7% for target emotion, 77.9% for intensity, and 80.8% for the ten cue dimensions, with Fleiss’ κ \kappa values of 0.65, 0.50, and 0.60, respectively ( Fleiss, 1971 ) . On the test set, agreement between the two full-coverage annotators is 81.7%, 75.5%, and 80.2%, with Cohen’s κ \kappa values of 0.54, 0.50, and 0.58, respectively ( Cohen, 1960 ) . These agreement levels characterize the reliability of the human annotations used to construct the reference labels for evaluating the automated judgments (Table D.1 in Appendix D and Table 2 ). sections.heading: Automated–Human Agreement.
sections.text: Table 2 reports agreement against the first-pass and the reviewed human reference. Against the first-pass reference, agreement is substantial on target emotion and the ten cue dimensions ( κ = 0.59 \kappa=0.59 –0.67) and moderate to substantial on conditional intensity ( κ = 0.58 \kappa=0.58 –0.76); against the reviewed reference it is 2–14 points higher, reflecting the 308 and 297 fields revised at review and, on the test set, the 41 videos that receive a label only after review (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Model-Level Consistency.
sections.text: Aggregate automated and human scores differ by at most 4 percentage points on the two development-set models and by 4–6 points on the test-set model, where automated scores are conservatively lower. Across model–emotion cells, Spearman correlation is 0.94 for target emotion and 0.90 for cue pass rates across model–emotion–dimension cells, indicating strong cell-level consistency across the three human-annotated generators and eight emotions even where absolute scores shift slightly.

sections.heading: Judge-Backbone Sensitivity.
sections.text: Applying an independent Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash evaluator to the 224 test-set videos under the same frozen protocol yields moderate to substantial agreement with Gemini across target emotion, joint intensity, the ten cue dimensions, and sound ( κ = 0.62 \kappa=0.62 –0.68), and comparable agreement with the first-pass human reference (Appendix D.5 ). On this test-set generator, the evaluation patterns are therefore not tied to a single evaluator backbone; cross-evaluator replication of the full 12-model benchmark remains future work.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce EmoTrace-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark for emotion generation in text-to-video models. It evaluates target emotion, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual cue dimensions using controlled prompts that vary intensity, cue specification, and linguistic realization. Experiments on twelve T2V models show that emotion generation, intensity control, and cue realization are distinct capabilities. Overall, EmoTrace-Bench provides a structured way to localize emotional generation failures to emotion category, intensity, and specific expressive cues, offering a more interpretable basis for evaluating and improving controllable emotional video generation.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Generative AI systems played two distinct roles in this work. First, the 12 text-to-video models evaluated in the benchmark were the objects of study; Gemini 3.1 Pro was used as the automated evaluator under the protocol described in Section 3.3 , and Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash (API ID: qwen3.8-omni-flash ) was used as a second evaluator in the backbone-sensitivity analysis (Appendix D.5 ). Their outputs were compared against human annotations and were not treated as ground truth. sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: The study evaluates model-generated videos and includes human annotation of 1,120 videos, of which 896 are used for development-set validity analysis and 224 form the test set. The annotation activity underwent a compliance review by the Kling Team and was determined not to require formal review by an institutional review board or independent ethics committee; this determination should not be interpreted as a formal IRB exemption. All annotators were adults who were informed about the task and participated voluntarily. They were compensated, and they could skip content or withdraw from the task. None of the annotators, including the two senior reviewers, are authors of this paper. The submission does not include annotator-level provenance or annotator demographic information. Because the benchmark covers anger, fear, disgust, and sadness, annotators could encounter negatively valenced generated content. EmoTrace-Bench may have dual-use implications: a diagnostic method for identifying the cues that convey emotion could also be used to make generated media more emotionally persuasive. We therefore recommend that cue-level automated scores not be used as optimization targets without human validation. The benchmark is intended for transparent evaluation and analysis of model behavior rather than for profiling individuals or inferring emotions from real people.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Section 3 specifies the prompt construction, structural verification, evaluation information boundaries, automated evaluation procedure, human annotation protocol, aggregation rules, and metric denominators used in this study. The project repository ( https://github.com/Tonyheng6/EmoTrace-Bench ) contains all 448 prompts and their per-prompt metadata, together with the frozen system prompts and decision rules of the automated evaluator. Sample-level human reference labels and annotator-level provenance are not released; the appendix reports the consensus-construction procedure and aggregate agreement statistics. These materials are provided so that the reported prompt structure and aggregate results can be independently inspected.

sections.heading: A.4 Retention and Failure Handling
sections.text: The protocol retains weak, off-target, visually poor, or otherwise unsuccessful generations because these are model outcomes rather than technical failures. Only process failures—for example, an unrecoverable provider error or a file that remains undecodable after retry—are separated from generation quality. Transient network, provider, and decoding failures are retried under the same frozen request settings. A sample that remains invalid is marked unscorable , logged separately, and removed from the relevant denominator; it is never converted into a negative emotion label. Safety refusals and corrupted media are likewise logged as failure types rather than silently replaced by a preferred candidate. The release manifest links every valid output to its model designation, prompt identifier, prompt hash, and media path. This one-to-one mapping supports an audit of the expected 12 × 448 12\times 448 grid without exposing model identity to either the automated evaluator or human annotators.

sections.heading: C.1 Three-Level Evaluation
sections.text: Automated evaluation and human annotation share one ordered protocol. First, the rater decides whether the specified target emotion is present. This is a binary verification task, not free classification among the eight emotions. Second, if the target emotion is present, the rater classifies its perceived intensity as weak or strong; if it is absent, intensity is recorded as not_matched rather than forced. Third, the rater independently determines whether each of ten audiovisual channels contains directly observable evidence supporting the target emotion. The three outputs answer different questions and are not converted into one another. In particular, target-emotion success and intensity are judged directly, not inferred from the number of positive cue channels. Likewise, a video may contain a local cue related to the target emotion without expressing that emotion clearly at the video level.

sections.heading: C.3 Shared Decision Rule
sections.text: A cue channel is labeled 1 only when all five of the following conditions hold: 1. the evidence is directly observable in the video; 2. the evidence belongs to the channel being judged; 3. the evidence clearly supports the specified target emotion; 4. the evidence is not an ordinary, neutral, or incidental occurrence; and 5. the evidence can stand without borrowing evidence from another channel. The following cases are explicitly labeled 0: no relevant evidence; evidence that is very weak or very brief; evidence that is occluded or unreadable; ambiguous meaning; a conclusion available only from the hidden prompt; a conclusion requiring an imagined backstory; evidence that depends on another channel; evidence closer to a neutral state; or evidence closer to another emotion. The modality boundary is part of the rule. C1, C2, V1–V4, X1, X2, and T1 are judged from the picture without using the soundtrack. A1 is judged from the soundtrack without using the picture. A close-up does not by itself satisfy C1, visible movement does not by itself satisfy C2, and a reaction without a visible cause does not satisfy X2. T1 requires the target emotion itself to persist, change, or develop; camera motion, color change, or an event transition alone cannot substitute for emotional development. Emotion-specific rule cards refine these channel-level rules. For example, a sadness–face decision requires a readable facial configuration rather than a single generic cue such as looking down, one tear, or a blue-gray palette. The same visible event can therefore receive different labels for different target emotions, but the shared five-part criterion remains fixed.

sections.heading: C.4 Information Boundary and Automated Evaluation
sections.text: Both evaluation pathways can access the full video, its native audio track when present, and the name and definition of the target emotion. Both are blinded to the generation model, full generation prompt, requested intensity, prompt template, explicit/implicit metadata, paired sibling video, and all other ratings. Revealing the target emotion turns the first decision into target verification; hiding the target intensity prevents the strong/weak decision from copying the requested label. Each of the 5,376 videos receives one automated evaluation pass using Gemini 3.1 Pro with temperature 0. Videos are sampled at 8 fps, and the pass consists of two separate calls under the frozen protocol above: the first call returns the target-emotion decision and, when the target is present, its perceived intensity; the second call returns the ten cue-channel judgments. No voting or cross-call aggregation is applied to the 12-model results; the two additional development-set runs (Appendix D ) serve only to verify stability. Because emotion and intensity are returned together within the first call, their separation is procedural rather than an architectural claim that one output cannot influence the other; the cue judgments are produced in a separate call that does not receive the first call’s output. Two bounded auxiliary modules supply measurement summaries. The visual-dynamics module summarizes cross-frame motion for V4, and the audio module summarizes track intensity and spectral properties for A1. Neither module receives the target emotion, requested intensity, or target labels; neither emits a channel label. The automated evaluator makes the final decisions from the complete video and may not treat an auxiliary summary as a substitute for observable emotional evidence.

sections.text: For a valid channel d d , cue support is measured only among videos in which the target emotion succeeds: Q d ​ ( m ) = ∑ p ∈ P m M m ​ p ​ Y m ​ p ​ d ∑ p ∈ P m M m ​ p . sections.heading: C.7 Bootstrap, McNemar Tests, and Multiplicity
sections.text: Uncertainty in target-emotion performance is estimated with 5,000 prompt-level paired bootstrap resamples. The same resampled prompt indices are applied to every model, preserving the matched benchmark design. The six reported Emotion tiers are based on 95% bootstrap intervals for paired differences. Models within a tier are not ordered, and tier assignments on a bootstrap boundary are marked as seed-sensitive. The six pre-specified template contrasts (Table B.3 , contrasts 1–6) are analyzed separately for each model. Each condition contains 32 videos. The binary outcome is joint E+I success, and the two matched conditions are compared with an exact paired McNemar test. The six planned tests within a model form one family and are adjusted with Holm’s step-down procedure at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . Effect sizes and confidence intervals are reported alongside adjusted significance. Given the small cells, a nonsignificant contrast is treated as inconclusive rather than as evidence that the two prompt forms are equivalent.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.15452v1 [cs.CV] 11 Oct 2026 EmoTrace-Bench: Diagnosing Emotional Expression in Text-to-Video Generation through Controlled Cues and Intensity Yeheng Wang Affiliation: Communication University of China, Beijing, China Affiliation: Equal contribution Liudan Shi Affiliation: Communication University of China, Beijing, China Affiliation: Equal contribution Yi Zheng Affiliation: Communication University of China, Beijing, China Email: zhengyi7592@cuc.edu.cn Affiliation: Corresponding author Jingke Li Affiliation: Kling Team, Beijing, China Shiyuan Liu Affiliation: Kling Team, Beijing, China Xin Tao Affiliation: Kling Team, Beijing, China Yuanxing Zhang Affiliation: Kling Team, Beijing, China Guoyu Sun Affiliation: Communication University of China, Beijing, China Abstract Text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly used to generate videos with targeted emotional expressions, yet existing evaluation methods mainly rely on holistic video–text alignment and provide limited insight into whether failures arise from target-emotion expression, intensity control, or specific affective cues. We introduce EmoTrace-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark that controls emotion intensity and selected affective cues in prompts and evaluates generated videos at multiple levels. EmoTrace-Bench contains 448 controlled prompts covering eight emotions, two intensity levels, and diverse cue conditions. Using 12 T2V models, we generate 5,376 videos and evaluate target-emotion presence, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual dimensions of emotional expression with an automated evaluator calibrated and validated against human annotations on a subset of the data. Results reveal substantial differences across models and prompt designs. Prompts that explicitly describe a character’s emotional reaction are followed more reliably than prompts that describe only events or scenes, whereas adding more affective cues or using more explicit cinematic audiovisual language does not consistently improve emotional generation. These results illustrate how aggregate alignment scores may overlook localized differences in target-emotion expression, intensity control, and cue realization. EmoTrace-Bench provides a traceable and interpretable framework for diagnosing emotional video generation without modifying existing generation pipelines, and we release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules. 1 Introduction Figure 1: EmoTrace-Bench at a glance. Left: the three-level evaluation taxonomy—whether the target emotion is expressed, whether its perceived intensity is weak or strong, and which of ten expression channels (character, visual form, audio, context, temporal) provide the evidence. Top right: correct content does not guarantee emotional expression; a model must infer the emotion from context and reaction and realize the requested intensity, and existing benchmarks do not diagnose where this fails. Bottom right: the four capability facets examined in Section 4—breadth across emotions and prompt conditions, depth of intensity control and cue support, and explicit versus implicit cue expression. Generating videos with explicit emotional expression is an important capability for controllable content generation in text-to-video (T2V) models. For controllable emotion generation, the key question is not only whether a video presents the target emotion, but also whether it follows the prompt’s requirements regarding the emotion category, emotion intensity, and specific expressive cues. Emotion generation in T2V is therefore not a single-dimensional problem; rather, it simultaneously involves multiple interrelated yet distinguishable capabilities, including emotion category, emotion intensity, and specific emotional cues. However, existing T2V evaluations have difficulty effectively distinguishing these capabilities. Existing multidimensional video generation benchmarks mainly focus on semantic consistency, visual quality, motion performance, and compositional relationships, and they generally lack explicit modeling of emotional expression ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ) . The few works oriented toward emotion generation also mostly use aggregate scores to measure the overall match between generated videos and emotion prompts ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) . Although these metrics can indicate whether a video aligns with its prompt overall, they provide limited insight into the specific causes of mismatches and may collapse qualitatively different generation errors into similar aggregate scores, thereby obscuring meaningful differences in models’ ability to follow fine-grained emotional instructions. As a result, such evaluations cannot fully characterize a model’s controllability over emotion category, intensity, and mode of expression in practical content creation. Adding more output-side metrics alone is insufficient, because confounds often arise during prompt construction. Emotional prompts typically combine multiple cues, making it difficult to attribute output changes to specific factors. Differences across emotion categories can further confound intensity comparisons. Reliable diagnosis therefore requires controlled inputs as well as fine-grained outputs. We propose EmoTrace-Bench (Figure 1 ), which treats prompts as controlled experimental variables. It varies two main factors: affective cues and emotion intensity. Cue-controlled prompts change only one cue phrase while keeping the rest fixed, with additional paraphrased variants to test sensitivity to wording. Intensity-controlled prompt pairs differ only in intensity-related terms while preserving the emotion category, scene, and other content. This design enables separate analysis of emotion category, intensity, and specific cues. Figure 2 summarizes the overall pipeline. At the output, we annotate target-emotion success, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual cue dimensions. Using 448 controlled prompts, we generate 5,376 videos from 12 T2V models and collect human annotations for 1,120 videos from three of them to validate the automated evaluation. The analysis reveals that emotion-category generation and intensity control are distinct capabilities, model performance can be sensitive to cue wording, and automated evaluation agrees broadly with human judgments while small systematic differences remain on some fine-grained dimensions. By controlling variables at the input and conducting fine-grained diagnosis at the output, EmoTrace-Bench decomposes emotion-generation performance that was previously mixed together in overall scores into more specific dimensions and prompt factors. At the same time, through per-video, per-attribute comparisons between human and automated evaluation, it further reveals the scope of applicability and limitations of automated evaluation across different emotional dimensions. The main contributions of this paper are threefold: (i) We introduce EmoTrace-Bench , a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark for emotion generation in text-to-video models. It decomposes emotion generation into three complementary levels: emotion category, emotion intensity, and ten affective cue channels, enabling localized diagnosis of generation failures. (ii) We develop a controlled prompt-construction framework that independently varies emotion intensity and affective cues under a minimal-difference design. It also includes semantically matched cue variants with different linguistic realizations, allowing us to study prompt sensitivity while reducing confounding across input factors. (iii) We benchmark 12 text-to-video models on 448 controlled prompts, yielding 5,376 generated videos, and collect human annotations for 1,120 videos to validate the automated evaluation protocol. Our analysis reveals substantial differences across models in emotion-category generation, intensity control, and prompt sensitivity, while showing that aggregate automated judgments are broadly aligned with human annotations. We release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules. 2 Related Work 2.1 Text-to-Video Generation Evaluation T2V evaluation has evolved from overall quality assessment toward multidimensional diagnosis. VBench, VBench++, VBench-2.0, EvalCrafter, and Video-Bench evaluate visual quality, motion, temporal consistency, subject consistency, spatial relations, text alignment, and higher-level generation fidelity ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ) . VABench and T2AV-Compass further consider audio quality and audiovisual consistency ( Hua et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) , while T2V-CompBench uses controlled prompts to evaluate compositional generation ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Despite this progress, these benchmarks mainly target general generation quality, semantic adherence, and compositionality. Emotional expression is rarely modeled as a structured capability with separable dimensions. Existing evaluations therefore provide limited diagnosis of whether errors arise from emotion category, intensity, or specific character, scene, and audiovisual cues. 2.2 Emotional Video Generation and Controllable Expression Recent work has begun to study emotion-aware video generation. EmoVid provides a multimodal dataset for emotion-centric video understanding and generation ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) ; FG-ECVG explores fine-grained controllable emotional video generation ( Wei et al., 2025 ) ; and EmoTalker studies editable emotional expression in talking-face generation ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . EmoWorld further disentangles atmosphere, affective semantic cues, and temporal progression, showing that video emotion contains multiple controllable components ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . These works mainly focus on emotional data, generation, or model-side control. Their evaluations still commonly rely on emotion-recognition accuracy, condition matching, or aggregate scores. Such metrics may assign similar scores to different failures, such as generating the correct emotion at the wrong intensity or creating an appropriate atmosphere without the requested facial or bodily expression. Thus, an overall emotion score is insufficient for diagnosing fine-grained emotional controllability. 2.3 Fine-Grained Emotional and Audiovisual Cues Emotion is conveyed through multiple channels. Psychological studies highlight the roles of facial expression, body posture, and movement ( Ekman & Friesen, 1978 ; Cohn et al., 2007 ; Coulson, 2004 ; Dael et al., 2012a ; Dael et al., 2012b ; Aviezer et al., 2012 ) , while film studies show that shot scale, motion, lighting, color, sound, and music also shape emotional perception ( Bálint et al., 2018 ; Detenber et al., 1998 ; Chion, 1994 ; Cohen, 2010 ; Bordwell et al., 2020 ) . Recent benchmarks such as Stable Cinemetrics and FilmBench evaluate structured cinematic attributes ( Chatterjee et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , while HVEval and HUG-VIS examine human-centered appearance, action, and emotion ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Building on these directions, EmoTrace-Bench decomposes emotion generation into emotion category, emotion intensity, and specific affective cues. It combines controlled prompts with fine-grained output evaluation to diagnose whether the target emotion is generated, whether its intensity follows the prompt, and through which character, scene, and audiovisual cues it is expressed. This moves emotion-generation evaluation from holistic matching toward traceable fine-grained diagnosis. Prompts from the controlled suite (top) are sent unchanged to every model; the middle row shows matched weak/strong generations for one fear prompt pair across models. All videos are scored by a single automated evaluator that is frozen after calibration against human labels (left) and applied through the two-stage affective evaluation (bottom). 3.1 Evaluation Target Design EmoTrace-Bench evaluates emotional video generation at three levels: target emotion, perceived intensity, and affective cues. We first define the target emotion set and then specify the audiovisual dimensions used for fine-grained diagnosis. Selection of Eight Emotions. EmoTrace-Bench includes eight emotions: amusement, excitement, awe, contentment, anger, fear, disgust, and sadness. The selection follows the discrete emotion set established by Mikels et al. using the International Affective Picture System (IAPS) ( Mikels et al., 2005 ) . It contains four positive and four negative emotions spanning different typical arousal levels ( Russell, 1980 ) . Three-Level Evaluation. For each generated video, the first level determines whether the target emotion is expressed. The second evaluates perceived emotion intensity as strong or weak when the target emotion is present, and as “not matched” otherwise. The third identifies which audiovisual cue dimensions support the target emotion. These levels capture whether the intended emotion is expressed, how strongly it is expressed, and through which cues. Multidimensional Affective Cues. Emotional expression in video can arise from character behavior, environmental context, and audiovisual form. Drawing on theories of emotional expression, film form, and an external inventory of affective cues ( Smith, 2003 ) , we define ten dimensions: facial expression, bodily behavior, lighting, color, composition, visual dynamics, temporal organization, sound, scene, and event. We retain cues that can be directly observed and judged relatively independently in short videos, while excluding factors that require long-form narrative, dialogue semantics, or broader temporal context. Operational definitions and channel-specific prerequisites are provided in Appendix C (Table C.1 ). 3.2 Controlled Prompt Set EmoTrace-Bench uses controlled prompts to vary emotion intensity, affective cues, and prompt formulation while minimizing unrelated changes across conditions. Scale and Structure. Each prompt is represented as P ⁡ ( e , s , i , t ) = B ⁡ ( e , s ) + I ⁡ ( e , i ) + ∑ d ∈ ℳ t C d , t ​ ( e , s ) , P(e,s,i,t)=B(e,s)+I(e,i)+\sum_{d\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}C_{d,t}(e,s), where e e is the target emotion, s s the scene, i i the intensity level, and t t the prompt template. B ⁡ ( e , s ) B(e,s) is the shared base description, I ⁡ ( e , i ) I(e,i) specifies emotion intensity, and C d , t ​ ( e , s ) C_{d,t}(e,s) denotes the realization of affective cue d d under template t t . The template determines which cue segments are included through ℳ t \mathcal{M}_{t} and, for selected conditions, how the same affective content is linguistically expressed. The benchmark crosses 8 emotions, 2 intensity levels with 2 samples each, and 14 prompt templates, yielding 448 prompts. The templates include emotion-only prompts, individual facial, bodily, scene, and event cues, combinations of character and environmental cues, alternative linguistic realizations, facial changes, empty scenes, and prompts containing all explicitly writable cues. Eight of the ten evaluation dimensions—facial expression, bodily behavior, lighting, color, composition, visual dynamics, scene, and event—can be explicitly specified in prompts. Temporal organization and sound are evaluated only in the generated video. Each prompt records whether a cue dimension is explicitly specified or left unspecified but observable, allowing explicit instruction following to be distinguished from cues that emerge without being requested. Representative prompt conditions are shown in Figure B.1 in Appendix B . Alternative Linguistic Realizations. To examine sensitivity to prompt formulation, we construct controlled prompt pairs that express similar affective content using different linguistic realizations. These pairs preserve the target emotion, scene, and intended affective content while changing how that content is described. They therefore allow us to test whether semantically similar instructions lead to different generation outcomes. Prompt Control and Validation. We apply three constraints to reduce unintended variation. First, strong–weak pairs share the same emotion, scene, base description, and template and differ only in preregistered intensity expressions; all 224 / 224 224/224 pairs pass character-level structural verification. Second, cue segments are reused across templates whenever possible. Of 384 reused segments, 372 are identical and 12 differ only in pronoun disambiguation; all 384 match after normalization. Third, controlled template pairs vary only the preregistered prompt factor, and all 448 prompts have unique SHA-256 hashes. These checks (Table B.4 ) establish structural consistency for controlled comparisons. 3.3 Automated Evaluation and Human Annotation Protocol Automated evaluation and human annotation follow the same three-level decision structure and information boundaries. Shared Evaluation Protocol. Both evaluators first determine whether the target emotion is present. If present, perceived intensity is labeled as strong or weak; otherwise it is labeled “not matched.” Each of the ten affective cue dimensions is then judged independently as present or absent in support of the target emotion. Emotion and intensity are judged directly and are not inferred from cue labels. Both evaluators see only the generated video, including its native audio, and the name and definition of the target emotion. They do not have access to the generation prompt or other metadata. The target emotion is provided because the task evaluates whether a specified emotion is expressed. The target intensity is hidden to reduce label-following bias. Automated Evaluation. All 5,376 videos are evaluated once using Gemini 3.1 Pro with temperature 0 under a frozen two-stage protocol: the first stage judges target emotion and perceived intensity, and the second stage judges the ten cue channels (Appendix C ). Videos are sampled at 8 fps. Auxiliary programs provide measurement summaries for visual dynamics and sound using cross-frame motion and audio features, respectively. The resulting single-run outputs are used for all 12-model benchmark results. To assess evaluator stability, we conduct two additional evaluation runs on the 896-video development set. Development-set validity results are reported as the mean over the three runs (Appendix D ). Wan-2.2, HunyuanVideo-1.5, Kandinsky-5.0-T2V-Pro, and LongCat-Video-13.6B do not provide usable native audio, so the sound dimension and Full 10D aggregate are not reported for these models. Human Reference and Consensus. The human reference contains a development set for protocol calibration and a held-out test set for cross-generator validation. All first-pass annotations are collected without access to automated evaluation outputs. The development set contains 896 videos from two generation models. Two senior annotators independently label all videos. Their matching labels form the first-pass consensus, while disagreements are resolved by the majority of available labels from five additional trained annotators (Appendix D ). The test set contains 224 videos from a third generation model and was not used in protocol development. Two trained annotators provide full first-pass annotations and form the initial consensus. After the automated evaluator is frozen, senior annotators conduct a second review of both sets (Appendix D ). Reviewers see only the video and decision rules, without access to the generation prompt, model identity, target intensity, or automated outputs. Reviewed labels form the reviewed human reference, and fields without a reviewed label are excluded from analyses against it. Metric Computation. The joint emotion-and-intensity score is computed over all 448 videos per model. Visual 9D averages cue support over the nine non-audio channels and is available for all models; Full 10D adds the sound channel and is therefore reported only for audio-capable models (Appendix C ). Both are computed only for videos that successfully express the target emotion and should therefore be interpreted together with target-emotion accuracy. “Undecided” and “not applicable” labels are excluded from the corresponding denominators. 4 Results and Analysis We analyze EmoTrace-Bench from three perspectives. First, we compare 12 T2V models in terms of target-emotion generation, intensity control, and cue realization. Second, we use controlled prompt pairs to examine the effects of cue specification, cue combination, and linguistic realization. Third, we assess the reliability of the automated evaluator through comparisons with human judgments and an alternative evaluator backbone. 4.1 Emotion Generation and Intensity Control The 12 models exhibit distinct capability profiles. Target-emotion accuracy ranges from 49.3% to 87.0%, joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy from 29.9% to 55.1%, and conditional Visual 9D expression depth from 62.7% to 83.5%. Paired intensity-control success is substantially lower, ranging from 10.3% to 29.5%. Taken together, these results suggest that models are generally more successful at expressing the target emotion than at reliably controlling its perceived intensity. Figure 3 (a) summarizes the overall model results. Prompt-level paired bootstrap analysis of target-emotion accuracy (Appendix C ) yields six bootstrap-based groups of models for which no significant within-group differences are detected under the adopted procedure. Seedance-2.5 and Veo-3.1 form the highest-performing group. These differences are not an artifact of generation seed. Regenerating all 448 videos for Kling-3.0 under three generation seeds, with prompts and all other exposed settings fixed, moves target-emotion accuracy by 3.6 points (72.5–76.1%) and joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy by 3.8 points (45.5–49.3%), with no pairwise difference significant under exact McNemar tests (Appendix A.3 ). For this model and these three seed settings, the observed score ranges are approximately 7–11 times smaller than the corresponding cross-model spreads. Performance also varies across emotion categories (Figure 3 (b)). Contentment (85.9%) and amusement (85.3%) achieve the highest average target-emotion accuracy, whereas anger (52.2%) and fear (59.8%) are the lowest. Across the emotion categories included in our benchmark, the four positive emotions achieve 17.7 percentage points higher target-emotion accuracy on average than the four negative emotions, with the difference consistent in direction across all 12 models. Intensity control exhibits a different failure pattern. Across models, 17.9%–48.2% of strong–weak pairs receive the same perceived intensity, whereas reversals occur in at most 5.8% of pairs (Table E.3 , Appendix E ). Thus, when intensity control fails, it is much more often because strong and weak prompts produce the same perceived intensity. Figure 3: Emotion generation across 12 T2V models. (a) Overall performance: target-emotion accuracy (Emotion), joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy (Emotion + intensity; E+I in the text), Visual 9D and Full 10D cue support, and bootstrap group; models within a group are not ordered. (b) Target-emotion accuracy for each of the eight emotions. Scores are obtained from one blinded automated evaluation per video. Cue-level results reveal additional cross-model differences (Figure 4 , left; Table E.1 , Appendix E ). Visual dynamics shows the largest variation across models, followed by event/reaction, sound, and lighting, whereas temporal organization and facial expression vary less. Because human–automated agreement is only moderate for composition and scene/space (Appendix D ), we report these two channels descriptively without further cross-model interpretation. Overall, target-emotion generation, intensity control, and cue realization capture different aspects of model behavior. These results motivate reporting these dimensions separately rather than collapsing them into a single aggregate score. 4.2 Effects of Controlled Prompt Design We next examine how model outputs change under controlled prompt variations. The analysis focuses on three factors: explicit cue specification, cue combination, and linguistic realization. Per-model results for all 14 templates are reported in Table E.4 (Appendix E ). Explicit Cue Specification. Explicitly specifying character reactions produces the largest and most consistent gains. Adding a character reaction to a scene-only prompt improves joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy by 25–59 percentage points across models, with a mean gain of 45 points. Adding a reaction to an event prompt yields a 22–69 point gain, with a mean of 46 points. After Holm correction, these improvements are significant for 9/12 and 7/12 models, respectively. Current models therefore follow explicit facial and bodily reactions more reliably than they infer such reactions from scene or event context alone. For cues that are not explicitly specified, we still record whether they appear in the generated video. Figure 4 compares overall cue support with support under unspecified conditions. These results characterize cue co-occurrence only and do not support causal interpretation. Figure 4: Overall (left) and implicit (right) cue-expression profiles of 12 T2V models. Values are relative to the best model in each channel. Cue Combination. The benefit of adding a cue depends on which cue is added, not on how many are present. Adding a facial expression to a body-only prompt raises joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy from 40% to 64% on average (+24 points; significant for 2/12 models), whereas adding bodily behavior to a facial-expression prompt adds only 7 points (57% to 64%; significant for no model). Descriptively, facial expression contributes more than bodily behavior in this contrast. Likewise, the template that combines all explicitly writable cues (ALL_DYNAMIC, 64%) performs no better than the face-and-body prompt and only 2 points above the emotion-label baseline (EMO, 62%; Table E.4 ). Alternative Linguistic Realizations. Describing a scene by how it feels conveys emotion more effectively than specifying how it should be filmed. With a character present, experiential atmosphere descriptions reach 27% joint emotion-and-intensity accuracy on average, compared with 13% for matched cinematic instructions; 9/12 models favor the experiential form, 2/12 significantly after correction. In empty scenes the two formulations perform alike (38% vs. 37%). For short, single-scene prompts of this kind, experiential language elicited emotional expression more often in our data. All pre-specified contrasts use exact paired McNemar tests with model-wise Holm correction (Table B.3 ). Because each condition contains 32 videos (16 strong–weak pairs), we read these comparisons as diagnostic evidence of how models respond to specific prompt changes. 4.3 Agreement Between Automated and Human Evaluation Because the preceding analyses rely on automated scores, we compare the automated evaluator with human judgments at both the annotation and model levels. The evaluation uses a development set of 896 videos and a test set of 224 videos from a third generation model, held out from protocol development. Human Agreement. On the development set, pairwise human agreement is 85.7% for target emotion, 77.9% for intensity, and 80.8% for the ten cue dimensions, with Fleiss’ κ \kappa values of 0.65, 0.50, and 0.60, respectively ( Fleiss, 1971 ) . On the test set, agreement between the two full-coverage annotators is 81.7%, 75.5%, and 80.2%, with Cohen’s κ \kappa values of 0.54, 0.50, and 0.58, respectively ( Cohen, 1960 ) . On this test-set generator, the evaluation patterns are therefore not tied to a single evaluator backbone; cross-evaluator replication of the full 12-model benchmark remains future work. 5 Conclusion We introduce EmoTrace-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark for emotion generation in text-to-video models. It evaluates target emotion, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual cue dimensions using controlled prompts that vary intensity, cue specification, and linguistic realization. Experiments on twelve T2V models show that emotion generation, intensity control, and cue realization are distinct capabilities. Overall, EmoTrace-Bench provides a structured way to localize emotional generation failures to emotion category, intensity, and specific expressive cues, offering a more interpretable basis for evaluating and improving controllable emotional video generation. Ethics statement The study evaluates model-generated videos and includes human annotation of 1,120 videos, of which 896 are used for development-set validity analysis and 224 form the test set. The annotation activity underwent a compliance review by the Kling Team and was determined not to require formal review by an institutional review board or independent ethics committee; this determination should not be interpreted as a formal IRB exemption. All annotators were adults who were informed about the task and participated voluntarily. They were compensated, and they could skip content or withdraw from the task. None of the annotators, including the two senior reviewers, are authors of this paper. The submission does not include annotator-level provenance or annotator demographic information. Because the benchmark covers anger, fear, disgust, and sadness, annotators could encounter negatively valenced generated content. EmoTrace-Bench may have dual-use implications: a diagnostic method for identifying the cues that convey emotion could also be used to make generated media more emotionally persuasive. We therefore recommend that cue-level automated scores not be used as optimization targets without human validation. The benchmark is intended for transparent evaluation and analysis of model behavior rather than for profiling individuals or inferring emotions from real people. Sample-level human reference labels and annotator-level provenance are not released; the appendix reports the consensus-construction procedure and aggregate agreement statistics.
